title: Why Australian Politics Is Shifting Right, Not Left
gist: Rising far-right politics in Australia is not a rejection of mainstream values but, per Cas Mudde's framework, an extreme extension of them, meaning disillusioned voters driven by financial stress and housing shortages drift right rather than left because far-right narratives connect more directly to existing mainstream Australian values.

insights.claim: Common drivers cited for Australia's far-right rise -- financial stress, housing shortages, and frustration with government -- fail to explain why disillusioned voters move toward the far right specifically rather than the left.
insights.speaker: Ibolya Losoncz
insights.so_what: Investors modeling Australian political risk should not assume economic distress translates uniformly into either left- or right-wing populism; the direction depends on which narratives already resonate with mainstream values.
insights.quote: The reasons for the rise of far-right politics in Australia are often cited as financial stress, housing shortages, and frustration with the government. Yet this doesn’t explain why disillusioned voters are drifting toward the far right instead of the left.

insights.claim: Political scientist Cas Mudde's framework holds that radical-right politics is not a rejection of mainstream democratic values but an extreme, amplified version of them -- contradicting the common assumption that the far right is a foreign 'sickness' in an otherwise healthy political system.
insights.speaker: Ibolya Losoncz
insights.so_what: This framework implies far-right movements should be analyzed as amplifications of existing mainstream sentiment (e.g., on immigration, national identity) rather than externally imported ideology, changing how policy risk and social-cohesion risk get modeled for Australia.
insights.quote: “The radical right isn’t a rejection of mainstream values, it’s an extreme version of them.”
